themes.model: Mount Fuji is the highest mountain in Japan, at three thousand seven hundred and seventy-six meters. It's an active volcano, but it last erupted more than three hundred years ago. For centuries it has been a sacred place and a favorite subject of artists, and it became a World Heritage Site in 2013. In summer, many people climb it to watch the sunrise from the top. If you don't want to climb, I recommend the Fuji Five Lakes area, where you can see the mountain reflected in the water.
qs: When is the best season to see Mount Fuji?
qsm: Winter is the best season, because the air is clear and dry, so you can often see the mountain covered in snow from far away.

themes.model: Sushi is vinegared rice combined with fish or other toppings. It started as a way to preserve fish, and the style we know today, nigiri, became popular in Edo, now Tokyo, as a kind of fast food. Today you can enjoy it at a conveyor-belt restaurant for a reasonable price, or at a counter where the chef prepares each piece in front of you. A tip: you can eat nigiri with your hands, and dip the fish side, not the rice, into the soy sauce.
qs: What would you recommend to a visitor who cannot eat raw fish?
qsm: I would recommend cooked toppings such as grilled eel, egg, or shrimp, and vegetable rolls like cucumber rolls. Many restaurants also have fried or seared options.

themes.model: Hanami means cherry blossom viewing. In late March and early April, people gather under the cherry trees in parks to have picnics with friends, family or colleagues. The custom goes back more than a thousand years. The blossoms only last about a week, which reminds Japanese people that beautiful things don't last forever. Popular spots in Tokyo include Ueno Park and the Meguro River, which is lit up at night.
qs: What manners should visitors follow during hanami?
qsm: They should not shake or pick the branches, they should take their rubbish home, and they should keep the noise down, especially at night.

qa1.q: A tourist says Nakamise Street is too crowded. What would you suggest?
model: I would suggest coming early in the morning, before it gets busy, or exploring the quieter side streets around the temple, where there are traditional craft shops.

qa2.q: A tourist wants to take photos inside the main hall. What would you say?
qa2.ja: 案内士としての対応・説明
model: I would politely explain that photos are usually not allowed inside the main hall, out of respect for people who are praying, but they are welcome to take photos of the buildings from outside.

themes.model: The tea ceremony, or sado, is the traditional way of preparing and serving matcha, powdered green tea. It was developed in the sixteenth century by Sen no Rikyu. More than just drinking tea, it's about hospitality, respect and appreciating the moment. Every movement of the host has a meaning, and guests admire the tea bowl and the seasonal decorations. Many temples and cultural centers in Kyoto offer short experiences in English, so it's easy for visitors to try.
qs: What should a guest do before drinking the tea?
qsm: The guest bows to the host, picks up the bowl with the right hand, places it on the left palm, and turns it slightly so as not to drink from the front, which is a sign of respect.

themes.model: The Shinkansen is Japan's high-speed train, also known as the bullet train. The first line opened between Tokyo and Osaka in 1964, just before the Tokyo Olympics. Today trains run at up to three hundred and twenty kilometers per hour, and they are famous for being safe and punctual: the average delay is less than a minute. Visitors can save money with the Japan Rail Pass. I recommend buying a bento at the station and enjoying it on board.
qs: How would you explain the Japan Rail Pass to a visitor?
qsm: It's a pass for tourists that allows unlimited travel on most JR trains, including most Shinkansen, for seven, fourteen or twenty-one days. It's good value if you travel between several cities.

themes.model: Summer festivals, or natsu matsuri, are held all over Japan from July to August. Many of them began as prayers for good harvests or to keep away illness. At festivals, people wear yukata, light summer kimonos, and enjoy food stalls selling yakisoba and shaved ice. Some festivals have huge portable shrines carried through the streets, and many end with fireworks. Famous examples are the Gion Festival in Kyoto and the Nebuta Festival in Aomori.
qs: What advice would you give to a visitor going to a summer festival?
qsm: I would advise them to drink plenty of water because it's very hot, to carry some cash for the food stalls, and to arrive early to get a good spot for the fireworks.

tr.ja: 日本の温泉には、いくつかのマナーがあります。湯船に入る前に体を洗い、タオルはお湯の中に入れないようにしてください。
model: There are some rules of etiquette at Japanese hot springs. Please wash your body before you get into the bath, and don't put your towel in the water.

qa1.q: A guest with a tattoo wants to use a public hot spring. What would you do?
model: I would explain that some hot springs don't allow tattoos, so I would check in advance and recommend a tattoo-friendly hot spring, or a private bath that they can reserve.

qa2.q: How would you explain why people wash before getting into the bath?
qa2.ja: 案内士としての対応・説明
model: The bath is shared by everyone, so washing first keeps the water clean. It's a way of showing consideration for other people.

themes.model: Ramen is a noodle soup that came originally from China and developed into a uniquely Japanese dish. There are four main types of soup: soy sauce, salt, miso and pork bone, called tonkotsu. Each region has its own style, for example miso ramen in Sapporo and tonkotsu ramen in Fukuoka. In many shops you buy a ticket from a machine before you sit down. It's fine to slurp the noodles; it shows you're enjoying them, and it cools them down.
qs: Are there ramen options for vegetarians?
qsm: Yes, more and more shops offer vegetarian or vegan ramen with soup made from vegetables or soy milk. I would check the menu or ask the staff in advance.

themes.model: Japanese gardens are designed to represent nature in a small space. There are several types, such as stroll gardens, where you walk around a pond, and dry gardens, or karesansui, where raked gravel represents water. The most famous dry garden is at Ryoan-ji in Kyoto. The gardens change with the seasons, from cherry blossoms in spring to red leaves in autumn. I recommend visiting early in the morning, when it's quiet and you can really feel the calm atmosphere.
qs: What is the meaning of the rocks in a dry garden?
qsm: They can represent mountains or islands in the sea, but their meaning is not fixed. Visitors are encouraged to sit quietly and use their imagination.

themes.model: Manga are Japanese comics, and anime is Japanese animation. They are enjoyed by people of all ages in Japan, and they cover every kind of story, from sports and romance to history and science fiction. Many anime are based on popular manga. Fans from around the world visit Akihabara in Tokyo and Nipponbashi in Osaka to buy goods. I also recommend the Ghibli Museum, but you need to book tickets in advance.
qs: Why do you think manga and anime are so popular abroad?
qsm: I think it's because the stories are very creative and the characters are easy to relate to. Streaming services have also made it easy for people all over the world to watch them.

points: 固有名詞は説明をそえて(Kaminarimon, the Thunder Gate)

qa1.q: A tourist with a bad knee wants to visit Fushimi Inari. What advice would you give?
model: I would recommend walking only the first section, the famous Senbon Torii near the entrance. It's mostly flat, and it's the most photographed part, so they can still enjoy the atmosphere.

qa2.q: Why are there so many torii gates?
qa2.ja: 案内士としての対応・説明
model: Each gate was donated by a person or a company, usually to pray for success in business. You can see the donor's name and the date written on the back of each gate.
